798.heavy: full vowel vs reduced vowel (ə, ə̈): a penult containing a 'reduzierten Vokal' rejects the accent; no role stated for vowel length or coda consonants
798.dflt: Word beginning (initial): when the penult has a reduced vowel the accent 'wird auf den Wortanfang verlagert' (Alhoniemi 1988:85); by the literal rule this also covers words with no full vowel, which Alhoniemi does not treat separately or exemplify.
798.prule: In the Western (Hill) literary language the accent lies 'in general' on the penultimate syllable; if in a polysyllabic word the penult contains a reduced vowel, the accent is shifted to the beginning of the word ('auf den Wortanfang verlagert'). Of the cited non-harmonic example words (kukšemäš, ošemən, kužikä) Alhoniemi notes that the accent lies on the boundary i or e; he reports, without adopting it, the claim of some scholars that this is always so, and cites makleštä·räš, koeštä·räš, where a front vowel follows e 'ungeachtet des Akzents' (the accent there is on the penult).
798.srule: Not mentioned in Alhoniemi 1988 (Das Tscheremissische, pp. 84-95; the accent passages pp. 85-86 give one 'Akzent' per word and say nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress).

800.heavy: A priority hierarchy rather than a heavy/light binary: (1) high-pitched (lexical-tone) syllables, all of which take primary stress; (2) if the word has no high pitch, long vowels, all of which take primary stress; (3) if neither, the last voiced vowel. 800.prule: In a given word all high-pitched syllables have primary stress; if the word has no high pitch, the long vowels receive primary stress (more than one primary per word possible, e.g. ex. evidence_works.detail: Surface-phonology reanalysis of Garvin 1950 from the author's own fieldwork (main informant Mrs. Bertha Provost, Anadarko, Oklahoma; fieldwork summer 1965, academic year 1966-67, Nov. 1967 and April 1969; fn. 2-3, p. R20). Sets out the prosodic inventory the 1996 sketch builds on: 'a contrast between high pitched and non-high pitched vowels' plus a short/long/extra-long length contrast (p. R5), and argues in sec. 2.2.2 (p. R13) that Garvin's phonemic primary stress is high pitch: 'Garvin analyzed the distinction between high and low pitch as one of primary stress, and then thought he heard primary stress in every word. His examples of "variable" stress are forms which have all low pitches; it is therefore natural that he would record now one, now another syllable as stressed. But in words with one or more high pitched syllables, Garvin (1950) always marked stress on the high pitches. His minimal pair for stress is really one for pitch' (pair tite?esc?i 'He is a thief' / tite?e:c?i 'They are thieves', p. R13; fn. 5, p. R20: Garvin and Hill 1962 later recognized phonemic pitch as well). The secondary-stress statement ('Secondary stress, however, is almost predictable, occurring usually on every second vowel in either direction from the primary stress', sec. 1.2, p. R3) is Rood's summary of Garvin's description, not a first-hand rule. The paper gives no stress-assignment hierarchy and no long-vowel clause; p. R24 says the three-degree length contrast occurs 'in any syllable, and independent of stress or tone'.

morph.rootq: p.99 (sec. 2.5.4.15): "Words ending in a syllable with a long vowel, followed by a syllable with a short vowel are stressed on the long vowel. ... Words ending in a long vowel, such as deengkii 'electricity', are stressed on the syllable before the final long vowel. ... Other words in Yapese are stressed on the last syllable of the word." The rule is stated over the word, not the root, and suffixes take main stress: p.100 "Note that in the first sentence the suffix -eew (meaning 'two') is stressed, receiving the main stress, but in the second sentence the particle gow (also meaning 'two') is unstressed"; p.149 "Note that the stress on chuwqiyéew is not on the syllable -qíy…
morph.elicq: No procedure is stated ("Stress in Yapese is not well-understood", p.99; "the discussion of stress in the rules which follow is less well worked out than the description of other processes", p.98). The evidence cited is impressionistic: isolated citation forms marked with acute accents (p.99 list: chibíy, paqág, moeróes, m'agpáaq, rogón) explicitly contrasted with short sentences: p.149 "the stress on chuwqiyéew is not on the syllable -qíy (as it is in chuwqíy pronounced alone)"; p.100 "Stress in phrases and sentences is not well understood. For example, in the sentence: Ka ra chibiyeew. 'They two lifted it.' which is pronounced: /kàrchì byé:w/ ... Ka ra marweel gow. pronounced…
morph.stmt: Jensen gives no one-line typological label; as the grammar lays it out, Yapese has "a small number of prefixes which are used to derive new words" (p.111: locative p'ee-/ta-/too-, resultative maa-, human pi-, agentive taa-, diminutive sa-, plus intransitive ma- and prefixal CV(C)- reduplication), while all inflection on the word is suffixal (transitive -y/-g/-eeg, subject-number -eew/-eed, object-pronoun and possessive-pronoun suffixes: "In verb phrases with transitive verbs as head the subject number marker is suffixed to the verb... it is for this reason that this type of verb phrase is called a suffixed pronoun verb phrase", p.216); tense-aspect, negation, subject person, articles…

804.sec_quote: Words with more than two syllables may have what are called secondary stresses ... Long vowels generally get such secondary stress. So moeroes ‘savage’ actually has a secondary stress on the first syllable: mòeróes. Closed syllables also receive secondary stress. Thus m'àgpáaq ‘wedding’ ... A word may have more than one secondary stress. An example is marungaqgean ... /màrngàqgë́:n/.

evidence_works.work: Lynch 2000, Reconstructing Proto-Oceanic Stress (Oceanic Linguistics 39: 53-82)
evidence_works.detail: Comparative reconstruction article; its Yapese section (3.5.2 'Heavy-or-final', p. 64) is explicitly secondhand: 'Jensen (1977:92-94) says of stress in Yapese that it is generally on the final syllable. However, there are two cases where stress is penultimate: (i) when the penult is long and the vowel of the final syllable is short; and, quite strangely, (ii) where the final syllable is open and contains a long vowel-exclusively in borrowed words. (A word with a closed final syllable that has a long vowel has final stress.)' (p. 64). (ii) de:nki: 'electricity', ba:te: 'kapok'; default ti'biy 'to lift', ro'gon 'its way', m'ag'pa:? 'wedding', mar'we:l 'work', da:'na:y 'no, not') is given with no source other than that Jensen citation; five of the nine (sa:lap, de:nki:, chibiy, rogón, m'agpáaq) are the record's Jensen examples. Two details the entry does not carry: (a) case (ii) (final open long vowel, stress on the syllable before) is restricted to loanwords, and 'It has only closed final syllables in nonborrowed lexical morphemes' (p. 64), so in native words a 'final if heavy (CVC)' reading cannot be told apart from default final stress; (b) on p. 79 Lynch rephrases the system as 'default stress on the final syllable unless a nonfinal syllable contains the only long vowel in the word' and as rule '(b) languages like Yapese: assign stress to the rightmost syllable containing a long vowel; if there is none, assign stress to the last syllable' (p. 79). That rephrasing is long-vowel-based only, and Lynch's own definition of the class in sec. 3.5 (p. 63) is 'a heavy syllable (i.e., CV: or CVV)': CVC is not heavy in it, so it sides with Jensen's long-vowel wording against the StressTyp2 'all heavy syllables' reading recorded in corr; it generalises Jensen's penult case to any nonfinal long vowel (it would put stress on the antepenult of an H L L word with a single long vowel in the antepenult, which the entry's stress strings code as final), but Lynch offers no Yapese data beyond the (16) examples for that shape, so it is an analyst's reformulation, not evidence. Yapese is also classed as 'heavy-or-peripheral' on pp. 75-76.

806.heavy: a syllable 'involving a long vowel' (vowel length only; ST1 note = long vowels; Hayes 1997 (28f) 'All syllables containing long vowels must be stressed'). Closed syllables are not mentioned as heavy.
806.prule: Stress is assigned to the first syllable containing a long vowel; if the word has no long vowel, to the first syllable of the word. Dixon does not rank the stresses into primary vs secondary (ST1 remark: 'Dixon does not mention any distinctions of prominences among the stresses'); StressTyp2 reads the long-vowel/initial stress as the main stress.
806.srule: Further stresses fall on every second syllable before and after the stress placed by the Stress Assignment Rule (first long-vowelled syllable, else the initial syllable), so that stressed and unstressed syllables alternate through the word: SU or US disyllables, SUSU or USUS quadrisyllables, USU in all trisyllables, USUSU in all quinquesyllables. Dixon assigns all stresses by this one rule and does not grade them as primary vs secondary.

808.dq: Within the domain of the word, stress and pitch are combined to form three degrees of accent - primary or strong (1), secondary (2) and tertiary or weak (3).
808.heavy: long vowels: a long vowel 'pronounced as a long vowel' attracts the accent of the preceding syllable; in practice low aa attracts, high ii/uu are usually 'broken' into two short vowels and do not attract primary. A final consonant does not add weight (paarnpaarn, with final C, patterns 1 3 like a short-vowel disyllable).
808.prule: Default primary accent on the initial syllable (pattern 1 3 2 3 2 3; also when long vowels occur only in odd syllables). A long vowel in the second syllable, if pronounced long, attracts the primary accent onto it: optionally in disyllables (3 1: kartaa, yurnrtaa; loan kiitaa), 'ordinarily' in trisyllables when the vowel is aa (3 1 2: nyilaarti, piyaarri); high long ii/uu are instead (nearly invariably) broken and primary stays initial (1 3 2, 1 3 2 3). 'The same pattern... also holds when the first short vowel is replaced by a long vowel' (nguurraarri, kaayuurru; by inference 3 1 2 and 1 3 2 3 - the source prints no digits for these). It does NOT hold when a further long vowel stands in the third syllable: primary then stays initial, 1 3 3 2 (thathaarlaa, martuurraa, and three-long-vowel maapuurraa). Rules 'not hard and fast' (ngatyaarra patterns as if high, purniina as if aa).
808.srule: Basic pattern 1 3 2 3 2 3: after the initial primary accent, secondary accent (2) falls on every odd-numbered syllable (3rd, 5th...) and weak (3) on even-numbered ones; the same holds when long vowels stand only in odd syllables (thaarta; ngunhungkiirri 1 3 2 3). A long vowel 'broken' into two short vowels counts as two syllables in the alternation (ngunhungkiirri 1 3 2 3 ~ 1 3 2 3 2, nyiinnyiin 1 3 2 3, maapuu 1 3 2). When the primary is deflected onto a long second syllable the alternation continues from it (ngurnaapurraa 3 1 3 2; ngunhaangata given as 3 1 2 3). With a second long vowel in the third syllable the pattern is 1 3 3 2, the secondary falling on the final long vowel (thathaarlaa, martuurraa, maapuurraa).

809.dq: Foot assignment: parse the word from left to right into iambs. ... Mark a foot as extrametrical at the right edge of the word. ... Word layer construction: group feet into a right-headed word constituent.

809.heavy: light = open short-vowel syllable (CV); heavy = long vowel (CVV) or short vowel + coda consonant (CVC), word-final CVC written H in the Negev schemas (LH ɣa.nám, LLH za.lá.mah); superheavy (S = CVVC/CVCC) distinguished word-finally and always stressed there
809.dflt: All-light words: per (21e), stress the penult or antepenult, whichever is separated by an odd number of light syllables from the beginning of the word (analysis (23): left-to-right (LL) iambs, right-edge foot extrametrical, head of the rightmost visible foot): LL -> final (ki.tá, disyllable clause 21d), LLL -> penult (a.ʔá.ma), LLLL -> antepenult, LLLLL -> penult; i.e. located at the right edge by parity counted from the left, not a fixed default syllable.
809.prule: Stress a superheavy ultima; otherwise a heavy penult; otherwise a heavy antepenult; otherwise the ultima of a disyllable beginning with a light syllable (ki.tá, ɣa.nám); otherwise the penult or antepenult, whichever is separated by an odd number of light syllables from the nearest preceding heavy syllable or, lacking one, from the beginning of the word. Analysis (Hayes 1995:227): left-to-right iambs (LL),(LH),(H); rightmost foot extrametrical; right-headed word tree (main stress on head of rightmost visible foot).
809.srule: Not mentioned in Kager 2009 ('Stress', EALL vol. 4, author MS pp. 10-11, Negev section exx. 21-24, read in full). StressTyp2 codes the left-to-right iambic footing as covert: 'This pattern is used only for the sake of defining main stress. Secondary stress is absent on the surface'.

810.tone: Pitch accent (Kiparsky 2003: 'the pitch accent of most words'). A long vowel or diphthong bears either acute (VV́, accent on the second mora) or circumflex (V́V, accent on the first mora); on short nuclei the distinction is neutralized. -VC syllables have one accentable mora (TBU), -VV two; acute/circumflex distribution is predictable in non-final syllables ((4): acute in the antepenult, and in the penult iff the final syllable is bimoraic). Accent position: recessive default (penult if final syllable heavy, else antepenult) or lexical stem-final accent, never left of the recessive position.

820.dq: Regularmente o acento primário da palavra (e dos itens lexicais simples) ocorre na última sílaba da palavra. ... Nessas palavras, com quatro sílabas, observamos que o pé do lado direito leva o acento principal, e o acento do primeiro pé está reduzido ao acento secundário.
820.dloc: Roessler 2008, ch. II phonology: 'Estrutura silábica' p.59; Sammons quotation p.58; 'O Acento', 'Pé Rítmico' p.62; 'Palavra Mínima' p.63 + Fig.027 p.64; Figs 028-029 pp.65-66; 'Palavras lexicais complexas' p.66 + Fig.030 p.67
820.heavy: 'núcleo vocálico ramificado' (branching vocalic nucleus, V(V) incl. Vj as in [nẽj]) = bimoraic syllable able to host a whole bimoraic foot; CV is monomoraic; syllables are closed only by a branching nucleus (CVV), there are no coda-C closed syllables (p.59).
820.dflt: final syllable (of the root / simple lexical word)
820.prule: Primary word stress falls on the final syllable of the simple lexical word/root (right-headed bimoraic iamb at the right edge, End Rule right); but if the first syllable of a (disyllabic) simple lexical word has a branching vocalic nucleus (CVV, bimoraic) it takes the foot and the stress, the final light syllable being left as a degenerate/unparsed syllable (['nẽj.nã] 'grande'). Most simple words are disyllabic (.x); rare trisyllables are ((. x)) with final stress.
820.srule: Only in complex lexical words (compounds) of two bimoraic iambic feet (four syllables): the right foot carries the primary stress and the first foot's stress is reduced to secondary, i.e. secondary on the 2nd syllable, primary on the final ([a.ˌtʃi.pu.ˈrã] 'vaca', [tʃa.ˌtʃu.pu.ˈrã] 'porco doméstico', [ru.ˌpɨ.dʒi.ˈwa] 'colher'). Simple lexical words (2-3 syllables) carry a single, final stress; no rhythmic secondary stress is described.
820.quote: O ACENTO – Regularmente o acento primário da palavra (e dos itens lexicais simples) ocorre na última sílaba da palavra. Sammons já nota esse fato (1977, p. 19) e também a semelhança da estrutura acentual com a língua dominante (possivelmente superstrata - lexifier) Guarani. Existem alguns morfemas gramaticais (sufixos) que não são acentuados, enquanto outros levam acento. ... A primeira sílaba de uma palavra lexical simples é acentuada, caso ocorra um nucleo vocálico ramificado nesta sílaba, como em ['nẽj.nã] 'grande'. PÉ RÍTMICO – Assumo neste trabalho que o padrão rítmico do achê é iâmbico.…
820.loc: Roessler 2008, ch. II phonology: 'Estrutura silábica' p.59; Sammons quotation p.58; 'O Acento', 'Pé Rítmico' p.62; 'Palavra Mínima' p.63 + Fig.027 p.64; Figs 028-029 pp.65-66; 'Palavras lexicais complexas' p.66 + Fig.030 p.67

820.exq_: Apenas alguns itens lexicais do achê escapam do padrão acentual, como por exemplo a palvra ['ja.(m)bu] 'acima'. Esse palavra contém, de fato, um demonstrativo e como segunda sílaba o morfema gramatical átono /-bu/ COND ... Sammons (1977, p. 19) menciona exceções como a palavra ['ka.pɛ] 'floresta'. …

It may more be "intonation" that is causing the seeming variance.'. For tone the entry now rests on Roessler 2018, quoted in the tone block.

morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was elicited appears on the stress pages available (Roessler 2008 pp.58-59, 62-67); the evidence shown is isolated citation forms in tables, e.g. p.62 'A primeira sílaba de uma palavra lexical simples é acentuada, caso ocorra um nucleo vocálico ramificado nesta sílaba, como em ['nẽj.nã] 'grande'' and Fig.030 p.67 [a.ˌtʃi.pu.ˈrã] 'vaca'. morph.stmt: Exclusively post-root: 'Ache is the only TG language that lacks left periphery marking of lexical stems altogether. Ache grammar retains around 20 functional formatives, suffixes and postpositional clitics' (Rößler 2015 p.377); 'all typical TG prefixation is absent from Ache grammar' (p.372); TAM, negation, case (DOM/LOC), determiner, interrogative and focus are all enclitics or suffixes on an otherwise isolating, largely disyllabic-root lexicon.

822.dq: For the accent of the words the following notes may help. (a) in words composed of a v-c-v the accent is on the last vowel ... The position of the accent remains the same even when the word is suffixed, or prefixed as in the case of verbs.
822.dloc: Introduction pp. V-VI, ACCENT paras (8)-(14); TONE para (16)
822.prule: Accent falls on the stem (root) vowel: the initial vowel of V-initial nouns (a-/o-) is unaccented (V-CV -> final, VC-VC -> final, V-CV-CV -> medial), C-initial CVCV words accent the first (stem) vowel, and the accent does not move when suffixes or verbal prefixes are added (boŋo/boŋona, konyo/akonyo/akonyowu). Position is therefore fixed by morphological structure (root vs affix), not by syllable count.

823.prule: Word stress is morphological: every root carries stress, suffixes (except the negative suffix) and clitics are unstressed; adjectival and verbal roots are stressed on the root-initial syllable; nominal roots of one or two syllables usually root-initial; uninflected function words usually initial.
823.srule: None rhythmic: 'Words usually have one stress.' A second stress in a word arises only from a second stressed morpheme: the negative tense suffix is stressed when further suffixes follow (root + suffix both stressed; stress on the preceding syllable sometimes reduced), and reduplicated roots / reduplicated function words carry minor stress on the first element and the main stress on the second (mbarmb'arni, lawl'aw).

824.idn: Dangme (acoustic data: Ada dialect, Apronti's own speech); data: Data = 27 tonograms made by E. O. Apronti of his own speech (Ada dialect) for his 1967 London PhD; one idiolect; no place or date of collection stated in the article
824.tone: Dakubu 1974 treats Dangme prosody entirely as tone: three contrastive tones on monosyllables (ma H 'corn dough', M 'herring', L 'town'), high vs non-high as the primary contrast in longer tone groups, downdrift/key-lowering, downstep from floating low, floating high, group-initial lowered high. The words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur in the 8-page article (scan a full-text search, all pages). Adomako 2018 likewise gives syllable = TBU and H/M/L, with no Dangme stress statement (its only 'stress' hits are about metrical theory in general and reference titles).
